episode.episode: 7-15-26 - Hour 4 - If BYU defeats Notre Dame and Utah will they go 12-0 this season?
episode.showDescription: Cougar Sports with Ben Criddle (@criddlebenjamin) keeps you up-to-date on all things BYU Sports. We not only cover football & basketball, but we dive into recruiting, baseball, soccer, and more. For insight that you can't get anywhere else, tune into 103.9/ 98.3 FM. Monday-Friday from 2-6 PM MST. Follow us on social media @espnthefan & interact with us using #ESPNTheFan.
episode.episodeDescription: Ben Criddle talks BYU sports every weekday from 2 to 6 pm. transcript_window.text: Not as well as I'd like.
You know, as I mentioned, I've been in the seat about 18 months now.
We've made some some organizational structural changes to try to operate more like a business, like everybody's doing.
where we haven't needed an influx of cash or, you know, equity from outside groups.
You know, our focus is, I'm a firm believer in if you are strategic and thoughtful and you have a long runway, you can plan for the future and be really economically successful.
And we've not been able to do that because the rules and really the landscape is changing so quickly.
You really can't forecast out past six months from now.
And I think schools like TCU, you know, we've we've got 100 ,000 living alumni on the planet.
We you know, Arizona State's a great example.
I think they've got about 1 .9
million living alumni on the planet.
And when you when you need the masses to help you get through this NIL world, we're certainly at a little bit of a disadvantage from a number standpoint.
What we have in our favor is a burgeoning economical community in Fort Worth, Dallas.
really successful from a business standpoint.

So we're trying to capture the hearts and souls of Fort Worth, whether you're an Aggie or a Longhorn or a Horned Frog, if you are in and around Fort Worth, we want you to adopt us as your hometown team and, and therefore be part of the community fabric and create opportunities, not just for our football and basketball players.
Like we want to be really competitive in, in golf and tennis and soccer.
And we've, we've managed to do that.

But as a former baseball guy and Olympic sport person, like it is really important that our, goalkeeper feels that she has supported every bit as much as our quarterback because her five hours a day that she's putting in on her craft, it's just as important to her as it is for, for Jaden Craig who gets to play in front of 55 ,000 people.
And that's really important to me that we protect that and give them the opportunity and give them the, the sense that they matter for, for what we're trying to do.
And, and that's kind of a challenge now when, when there's these dollars are going towards really two or three main sports.
sports, it's hard to make people look them in the eye and say they matter a lot.
So we have to try to find ways to show them that.

In order to execute that then from a visionary standpoint and starting with the end in mind, if you will, is there virtue in separating football, men's football and basketball from the other Olympic sports?

You have your scholarship kind of Title Title IX policies and bylaws and laws you have to abide by, if you could separate that and have it as a standalone entity, and I'm not saying take on private equity or anything like that, but you can do it maybe executed through corporate sponsorships and things of that nature
that already buoy up the athletic department in some way, is there virtue in evaluating a separation of those revenue, profit -generating sports, do you think?
